newsitem.title: UK: TransCo confident UK gas Code will cope this winter.
newsitem.headline: TransCo confident UK gas Code will cope this winter.

text.p: TransCo, the division of British Gas Plc responsible for gas transport, is confident that the introduction of the Network Code will not have a negative impact on gas supplies this winter.

Chris Train, Manager, Service Development Strategy at TransCo, told Reuters he is "as confident as anybody can be" that the Network Code -- a new set of rules governing gas transport and trade in Britain -- will work.

The Code was introduced in two phases, in March and September this year. It governs relations between TransCo and gas shippers using the National Transmission System, or trunk pipeline network, now that any licensed shipper can use the network under the deregulated gas market.

The main provision for shippers is that they must balance inputs of gas to the system with offtakes sent to customers on a daily basis. Financial penalties are imposed for failure to balance, and these became more stringent under phase two of the Network Code, or "hard landing" on September 1. But uncertainty remains over how the gas industry will perform during the first winter under the code.

Train says that the financial penalties are working to ensure regular supply of gas. "The signs are very encouraging that the financial incentives are working," he said, although he added "we will have to see what happens when the weather turns cold".

In cases of extreme weather, some customers who buy cheaper gas on an "interruptible" basis face the prospect of having supplies cut. Interruptible contracts are sold on the understanding that buyers stop using gas if demand exceeds expectations, to ensure continuity of supply to customers buying full-priced gas on a "firm" or non-interruptible basis.

Train agrees some users may face interruptions this winter. "There is always the potential. An interruptible contract is there to supply peak shaving for the supply/demand match", he said, adding if interuptible buyers fail to stop using gas when instructed to, it could jeopardise other users.

Last winter, over 4,000 domestic users in Glasgow were cut off for five days when all Scottish interruptible sites were told to stop using gas on December 28. But in fact consumption among these users only fell by 60 percent and TransCo had to cut off supplies to some domestic users because of loss of pressure.
"Supplies to the whole of Glasgow were very much on the margins" said Andy McPhee, a grid operations manager at TransCo.

Ofgas, the industry regulator, issued a report last week on likely gas supply and demand for this winter and implications for customers. The report concluded that "strong financial incentives, introduced on September 1 1996 as part of the Network Code to make gas available at times of peak demand, means that in normal circumstances it is unlikely that customers who do not wish to be interrupted will be".

Ofgas also looked at the way in which interruptions were applied last winter and concluded that the process could be improved by better communications, although it added that there was no evidence of improper action by either TransCo or British Gas Trading.
